screens.title: Physics & Collision Detection in 3D
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of Unity's 3D physics toolkit and when to use each feature. Physics in Unity is driven by two cooperating systems: Rigidbodies, which let objects respond to gravity, forces, and impulses, and Colliders, which define the shape used for collision checks. You'll learn the difference between primitive colliders and mesh colliders, how triggers differ from physical collisions, and how to tune behavior with Physics Materials. We will also walk through two live-coded examples: a collectible using a trigger and a bouncing object that responds to collisions. Finally, we'll add raycasting to let the player select or interact with objects at range. Each of these pieces matters because they enable believable movement, performant collision checks, and precise player interaction. A common pitfall is forgetting a Rigidbody or misusing a mesh collider for moving objects — we'll show alternatives and best practices so your scenes remain responsive and fast. By the end, you'll be able to set up interactive collectibles, tweak bounce and friction, and use raycasts for line-of-sight interactions.

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will practice in the hands-on lab. First, you will explain how a Rigidbody and a Collider work together and why both are required for full physics interactions. For example, you will be able to describe why a collectible must be a trigger collider while the player needs a Rigidbody to detect it. Second, you will differentiate collider types and choose the right one for a use case: use Boxes, Spheres, and Capsules when you need performance and MeshColliders only when accuracy for static geometry is essential. Third, you will implement collision and trigger callbacks in C# to make mechanics like bouncing or picking up items; this includes writing OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter handlers and checking tags or interfaces. Finally, you will set up Physics Materials to control friction and bounciness, and use Raycasting with LayerMasks to select objects or check line-of-sight. Each objective ties to a concrete scene action so you graduate from concept to working gameplay behavior.

screens.title: Rigidbody Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: A Rigidbody is the component that makes a GameObject subject to Unity's physics simulation. In simple terms, adding a Rigidbody allows gravity, forces, and collisions to change an object's position and rotation through the physics engine rather than by direct transform manipulation alone. This matters because it produces natural motion, momentum, and predictable physical interactions. For example, a rolling ball needs a Rigidbody so gravity and friction make it slow down and roll realistically. Without a Rigidbody, a Collider alone will detect overlaps but not respond to forces; that is why static objects like scenery often have Colliders but no Rigidbody. Key Rigidbody properties include mass, which affects how much force moves an object; drag and angularDrag, which damp linear and rotational motion; and isKinematic, which tells Unity that the physics engine should not move the object. Using isKinematic is useful for objects you move by script or animation yet still want to register collisions with non-kinematic bodies, such as a moving platform that should push the player. A common misconception is to assume that adding a Collider alone will make an object movable by physics—without a Rigidbody, the physics engine will not apply forces or gravity. Takeaway: add a Rigidbody when you need simulated motion; choose kinematic when you want scripted control but still need collision interaction.

keyIdea.title: Rigidbody takeaway
keyIdea.text: Rigidbody enables simulated motion and forces; use isKinematic when scripted movement is required but collision responses to others are still needed.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Rigidbody Fundamentals
Definition
Rigidbody

A component that hands motion control to Unity's physics engine so gravity, forces, and collisions affect an object. It is required for realistic physical response.

Key Properties
  • mass — affects acceleration from applied forces.
  • drag / angularDrag — reduce linear and rotational motion over time.
  • isKinematic — disable physics-driven motion while still allowing collision interactions with dynamic bodies.
Concrete example

A ball needs a Rigidbody so gravity pulls it down, friction slows it, and collisions with the ground produce a bounce. A door you animate should be kinematic so it doesn't react to physics pushes yet still collides with other objects.

Common mistakes & checks
  • Assuming a Collider alone allows physics movement — it doesn't. Add a Rigidbody for simulated response.
  • Making everything non-kinematic can cause unstable stacks; use isKinematic for scripted movers.
  • Incorrect mass values can make forces feel sluggish or too strong; tune incrementally.
Key Takeaway

Add a Rigidbody when you want physics-driven motion; set isKinematic when moving an object by script but still needing collisions with others.

screens.title: Rigidbody Properties & Motion Tuning
screens.narratorSegment: Tuning Rigidbody properties transforms raw physics into usable gameplay. Mass controls how much force is required to change an object's velocity; heavier objects need more force to accelerate. Drag and angular drag simulate air resistance and rotational damping: add drag to slow sliding or to avoid perpetual motion after collisions. A practical pattern is to start with reasonable defaults, then adjust mass in proportion to expected forces. For example, if a player push applies a fixed impulse, increase the mass of heavy crates so they resist moving. The isKinematic flag is a special case: when set, the object no longer moves because of the physics simulation — you move it via script or animation — but it can still affect other non-kinematic rigidbodies through collisions. Use kinematic objects for moving platforms or doors that must be precisely controlled yet still interact with the player. A common misconception is treating drag as friction with the ground — drag is global velocity damping and not a substitute for friction between surfaces. When tuning, test collisions at runtime and observe relative velocity magnitudes to decide whether to apply impulses or alter mass and drag. Final takeaway: adjust these properties iteratively while playing the scene to find natural-feeling responses.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Tuning Rigidbody Properties
Step-by-step tuning
  1. Set reasonable defaults: mass 1, drag 0, angularDrag 0.05.
  2. Apply expected force in Play mode and observe acceleration.
  3. If object moves too easily, increase mass or reduce applied force.
  4. To reduce sliding after collision, increase drag.
  5. For scripted movers, enable isKinematic and move via Transform/Velocity in code.
Example scenario

You have a crate and a player push force of 5 units. If the crate mass is 0.5 it will fly away; raising mass to 5 makes the push feel realistic. If the crate keeps sliding after the push, increase drag to 1 to simulate friction-like damping.

Misconception check

Drag is not surface friction. Use Physics Materials on colliders to affect how surfaces slide against each other. Drag is global motion damping in the physics solver.

Key Takeaway

Tune Rigidbody values iteratively in Play mode; use isKinematic for script-driven movers that still need collision interaction.

screens.title: Collider Types & Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: Colliders tell the physics engine where an object exists. Unity provides fast primitive colliders — BoxCollider, SphereCollider, and CapsuleCollider — and a MeshCollider for detailed shapes. Primitive colliders are computationally cheap and are the preferred choice for moving objects because they allow the physics solver to calculate collisions quickly. Use a BoxCollider for crates or floors, a SphereCollider for round pickups, and a CapsuleCollider for characters since its shape approximates a standing humanoid well and provides smooth sliding against obstacles. MeshColliders use the object's mesh geometry and can be either convex or non-convex; they give precise collisions but at a significant performance cost. Non-convex MeshColliders cannot be used on moving Rigidbodies that collide with other non-convex MeshColliders, so they are typically reserved for static environment geometry like terrain and large architecture. Best practice: approximate complex meshes with a compound of primitive colliders whenever possible. For example, approximate a car with several boxes and spheres rather than a single MeshCollider to keep collision checks fast. A misconception is that mesh colliders automatically give better gameplay; often they introduce jitter or performance spikes if used on dynamic objects. Takeaway: prefer primitives for moving objects, reserve mesh colliders for static, detailed geometry.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Collider Types & Use Cases
BoxCollider

Fast and stable for rectangular objects like crates, platforms, and simple environment blocks.

Use when: geometric simplicity and performance matter.
SphereCollider

Ideal for round objects and quick overlap checks such as pickups and projectiles.

Use when: radial symmetry and cheap checks are needed.
CapsuleCollider

Great for characters because it slides smoothly and reduces snagging on edges.

Use when: approximating humanoid bodies.
MeshCollider

Offers mesh-accurate collisions but is heavier. Non-convex mesh colliders are limited in interactions with dynamic rigidbodies and should be used mostly for static environments.

Best practice: use compound primitives first, fall back to MeshCollider for static complex shapes only.

screens.title: Collision Events vs Trigger Events
screens.narratorSegment: Unity provides two overlapping detection models: collision callbacks and trigger callbacks. Collision callbacks — OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit — are used when physical contact and response are important. They return a Collision object with contact points and relative velocity, which you can use to respond physically, play impact sounds, or apply forces. For instance, to make a ball bounce off a wall and play a sound when impact is strong, check the Collision's relativeVelocity magnitude inside OnCollisionEnter and add an impulse or play audio accordingly. Trigger callbacks — OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit — are for overlap detection without physical obstruction. A Collider marked as Is Trigger will let objects pass through while still notifying scripts. Use triggers for pickups, zones that damage the player, or finish lines because they detect entry without changing motion. A frequent error is forgetting that at least one of the interacting objects must have a Rigidbody for callbacks to fire. Also, triggers do not produce contact points or relative velocity; they are purely for detection logic. Takeaway: use collisions when you need physical response and use triggers when you only need to detect presence or overlaps.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Collision vs Trigger
Collision callbacks

OnCollisionEnter/Stay/Exit fire when colliders make physical contact and at least one has a Rigidbody. Use the Collision data for impact response and physics effects.

  • Provides contact points and relative velocity.
  • Use for bouncing, damage on impact, or adding forces.
Trigger callbacks

OnTriggerEnter/Stay/Exit fire when an object enters a trigger volume. Triggers detect presence but do not block motion.

  • No contact points or relative velocity provided.
  • Ideal for pickups, zones, and objective detection.
Check your understanding

If a collectible doesn't trigger, confirm that either the collectible or the player has a Rigidbody and that the collectible's collider has Is Trigger checked.

screens.title: CollectibleItem Trigger Script
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simple trigger script for collectibles. The script checks when another collider enters the trigger, verifies that it belongs to the player via a tag, and then runs collection logic such as awarding points or destroying the item. This pattern keeps item logic self-contained and minimizes coupling between player and items. In practice, ensure the player GameObject has a Rigidbody and the collectible's collider has Is Trigger enabled. Also confirm tags are consistent. A common mistake is relying solely on object names or lacking a tag check, which can produce false positives; use CompareTag for reliable checks. When destroying the item, you might want to play an effect first, so call the effect before Destroy. This example is safe for runtime usage and scales when you add pooling or UX feedback. Try extending the script to notify a score manager or emit an event instead of directly destroying the GameObject if you need decoupled systems. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › CollectibleItem Script
Pattern explained
  • OnTriggerEnter receives a Collider for the entering object.
  • CompareTag guards logic so only the player triggers collection.
  • Perform UI/sound feedback before Destroy to ensure effects play.
Key Takeaway

Validate the collider's identity, play feedback, then remove or pool the item. This keeps gameplay responsive and maintainable.

Example code
using UnityEngine;

public class CollectibleItem : MonoBehaviour
{
  public string playerTag = "Player"; // Ensure your player GameObject has this tag

  void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
  {
    // Check if the collider entering the trigger belongs to the player
    if (other.CompareTag(playerTag))
    {
      Debug.Log("Player collected " + gameObject.name);
      // Here you would add logic for what happens when collected:
      // e.g., give points, play sound, update UI, destroy item
      Destroy(gameObject);
    }
  }

  void OnTriggerStay(Collider other)
  {
    // Optional: for visual feedback or other continuous effects
    // Debug.Log(other.name + " is still in the trigger area.");
  }
}

screens.title: Bouncing Ball & Collision Example
screens.narratorSegment: This example demonstrates physical collision handling and how to pair it with Physics Materials to create a satisfying bounce. In the code sample we require a Rigidbody and a Collider on the same object, then listen for OnCollisionEnter. We check collision. relativeVelocity magnitude to decide whether the impact is strong enough to trigger a bounce effect or play feedback. Separately, Physics Materials control friction and bounciness at the collider level. Create a Physics Material, set its bounciness to a value like one for a rubbery surface, and set Bounce Combine to Maximum to preserve high bounciness when colliding with other bouncy surfaces. A common mistake is assigning a 2D Physics Material in a 3D context — ensure you create a Physics Material for 3D physics. Also, adding force on collision can cause double-bounces if the material already returns energy; test and tune whether to rely on the material or script impulses. The practical workflow is: set up the material, observe bounce in Play mode, then refine with scripted impulses if you need directional or conditional bounce behavior. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Bouncing Ball Example
Practical steps
  1. Add Rigidbody and a primitive collider to the ball.
  2. Create a Physics Material with desired bounciness and assign it to the collider.
  3. Use OnCollisionEnter to detect strong impacts and optionally apply force or play effects.
Tip: If collisions feel jittery, check mass ratios and solver settings, and prefer primitive colliders on dynamic objects.
Example code snippet
[RequireComponent(typeof(Rigidbody))] // Ensures Rigidbody is present
[RequireComponent(typeof(BoxCollider))] // Or SphereCollider, etc.
public class BouncingBall : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float bounceForce = 10f;

screens.title: Physics Materials: Friction and Bounciness
screens.narratorSegment: Physics Materials let you control how colliders interact at their contact points. Two main properties are friction, which resists sliding between surfaces, and bounciness, which controls how much velocity is returned after a collision. Each material also has combine modes for friction and bounce — Average, Minimum, Multiply, and Maximum — that determine how two materials' properties mix on contact. For example, if one object has high bounciness and the other is low, the Bounce Combine mode determines whether the result is averaged, dominated by the maximum, or multiplied, which affects the final behavior. A practical example: an icy surface uses low friction to let objects slide, while a rubber ball uses high bounciness and a Maximum combine to keep lots of rebound energy. Avoid relying on physics materials alone to create directional bounces; use collision callbacks to add impulses for more control. Also note that 2D and 3D physics use different material asset types. Takeaway: use Physics Materials to define consistent surface interactions and choose combine modes intentionally when objects with different materials collide. screens.title: Raycasting in 3D
screens.narratorSegment: Raycasting is a non-physical detection method that sends an invisible line into the scene and returns the first collider it intersects. Use it for line-of-sight checks, object selection, interaction prompts, and ground detection. A Physics. Raycast call returns a boolean indicating a hit and can populate a RaycastHit struct with the hit object, impact point, and surface normal. Raycasts are efficient and precise because you control origin, direction, distance, and layer filtering. For example, for object selection from the camera, create a ray from the camera's center forward and use a LayerMask to include only interactable objects; this prevents accidental hits on UI or environment geometry. A common pitfall is not using LayerMasks, which leads to hitting unintended objects and extra processing. Also, raycasts do not replace collisions for physical simulation — they are detection tools. When using raycasts for ground checks, prefer short rays and consider using multiple rays or a small sphere cast to avoid false negatives on uneven terrain. Takeaway: raycasts give precise, low-cost detection when you need to ask questions about the scene without altering physics state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › PlayerInteraction Script
Interaction flow
  1. Create a ray from the camera center using ViewportPointToRay.
  2. Use Physics.Raycast with a LayerMask and max distance.
  3. On hit, log or show prompt; on click, call Interact if the object implements IInteractable.
Debug tip: use Debug.DrawRay to visualize the ray while in the editor.
Example code
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerInteraction : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float interactionDistance = 3f;
  public LayerMask interactableLayer; // Assign a layer for interactable objects

  void Update()
  {
    // Cast a ray from the camera's center forward
    Ray ray = Camera.main.ViewportPointToRay(new Vector3(0.5f, 0.5f, 0));
    RaycastHit hit;

    // Draw a debug ray in the Scene view (only visible in editor)
    Debug.DrawRay(ray.origin, ray.direction * interactionDistance, Color.red);

    if (Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, interactionDistance, interactableLayer))
    {
      Debug.Log("Looking at: " + hit.collider.gameObject.name);

      if (Input.GetMouseButtonDown(0)) // Left mouse click
      {
        IInteractable interactable = hit.collider.GetComponent<IInteractable>();
        if (interactable != null)
        {
          interactable.Interact();
        }
        else
        {
          Debug.Log("Hit object is not interactable.");
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

public interface IInteractable
{
  void Interact();
}

public class Door : MonoBehaviour, IInteractable
{
  public void Interact()
  {
    Debug.Log("Door " + gameObject.name + " opened!");
  }
}

screens.title: Hands-on Scene Setup
screens.narratorSegment: Follow these steps to construct the hands-on scene that demonstrates triggers, collisions, physics materials, and raycasting. First, create a Plane to serve as ground. Add a Capsule for the Player, name it Player, add a Rigidbody with Use Gravity enabled, and set its Tag to Player. Next, create a Sphere, name it Coin, add a SphereCollider and check Is Trigger, attach the CollectibleItem script, and duplicate the coin around the level. Third, make a Cube and scale it flat to create a BouncyPlatform. Add a BoxCollider and create a Physics Material named Bouncy with high bounciness and Bounce Combine set to Maximum, then assign it to the collider. Finally, add a simple Cube Door with a BoxCollider and a Door script implementing IInteractable, set its layer to Interactable, and attach the PlayerInteraction script to the player's camera with the interactable layer mask selected. When testing, verify that coins disappear on trigger, the player bounces on the platform, and looking at the door while clicking logs interaction. This structured setup helps you validate each concept independently before combining them into more complex systems.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Debugging Tips
screens.narratorSegment: When things don't behave as expected, a few quick checks usually identify the problem. First, ensure at least one of the colliding or overlapping objects has a Rigidbody — without it, collision and trigger callbacks won't run. Second, verify that triggers have Is Trigger checked and that you are using the correct callback type: triggers use OnTriggerEnter while physical impacts use OnCollisionEnter. Third, confirm that you assigned the correct Physics Material type for 3D physics; using a 2D material will have no effect. Fourth, watch out for MeshColliders on moving objects — they often cause performance issues or unexpected interactions; prefer compound primitive colliders for moving elements. Fifth, use LayerMasks with raycasts to prevent hitting unintended objects and to speed up checks. Helpful debugging tools include Debug. DrawRay to visualize rays and adding Debug. Log statements that show collision. relativeVelocity to tune bounce thresholds. Finally, when destroying objects in triggers, consider playing visual or audio feedback first or use object pooling to avoid allocation spikes. Takeaway: systematic checks for Rigidbody presence, collider settings, material type, and layer masks will resolve most common physics problems.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a practical understanding of Unity's 3D physics toolkit and when to use each feature. Physics in Unity is driven by two cooperating systems: Rigidbodies, which let objects respond to gravity, forces, and impulses, and Colliders, which define the shape used for collision checks. You'll learn the difference between primitive colliders and mesh colliders, how triggers differ from physical collisions, and how to tune behavior with Physics Materials. We will also walk through two live-coded examples: a collectible using a trigger and a bouncing object that responds to collisions. Finally, we'll add raycasting to let the player select or interact with objects at range. Each of these pieces matters because they enable believable movement, performant collision checks, and precise player interaction. A common pitfall is forgetting a Rigidbody or misusing a mesh collider for moving objects — we'll show alternatives and best practices so your scenes remain responsive and fast. By the end, you'll be able to set up interactive collectibles, tweak bounce and friction, and use raycasts for line-of-sight interactions.

These objectives map to practical skills you will practice in the hands-on lab. First, you will explain how a Rigidbody and a Collider work together and why both are required for full physics interactions. For example, you will be able to describe why a collectible must be a trigger collider while the player needs a Rigidbody to detect it. Second, you will differentiate collider types and choose the right one for a use case: use Boxes, Spheres, and Capsules when you need performance and MeshColliders only when accuracy for static geometry is essential. Third, you will implement collision and trigger callbacks in C# to make mechanics like bouncing or picking up items; this includes writing OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter handlers and checking tags or interfaces. Finally, you will set up Physics Materials to control friction and bounciness, and use Raycasting with LayerMasks to select objects or check line-of-sight. Each objective ties to a concrete scene action so you graduate from concept to working gameplay behavior.

This slide maps objectives to practice tasks so you know how to demonstrate each skill. To show you understand rigidbodies and colliders, you'll set up a Player capsule with a Rigidbody and several trigger Coins. To prove you can pick colliders correctly, you will replace an expensive mesh collider with combined primitive colliders and note performance changes. For scripting collisions, you'll implement OnTriggerEnter on collectibles and OnCollisionEnter on a bouncing object, checking relative velocity before applying effects. To show mastery of materials and raycasting, you'll create a Physics Material named Bouncy and apply it to a platform, then write a raycast from the camera to detect a Door object using a LayerMask. Each task has a simple acceptance test: coins disappear on trigger, bounce effect happens on strong collision, and raycast logs the hit object. These checks ensure you can not only explain the concepts but apply and test them in a Unity scene.

A Rigidbody is the component that makes a GameObject subject to Unity's physics simulation. In simple terms, adding a Rigidbody allows gravity, forces, and collisions to change an object's position and rotation through the physics engine rather than by direct transform manipulation alone. This matters because it produces natural motion, momentum, and predictable physical interactions. For example, a rolling ball needs a Rigidbody so gravity and friction make it slow down and roll realistically. Without a Rigidbody, a Collider alone will detect overlaps but not respond to forces; that is why static objects like scenery often have Colliders but no Rigidbody. Key Rigidbody properties include mass, which affects how much force moves an object; drag and angularDrag, which damp linear and rotational motion; and isKinematic, which tells Unity that the physics engine should not move the object. Using isKinematic is useful for objects you move by script or animation yet still want to register collisions with non-kinematic bodies, such as a moving platform that should push the player. A common misconception is to assume that adding a Collider alone will make an object movable by physics—without a Rigidbody, the physics engine will not apply forces or gravity. Takeaway: add a Rigidbody when you need simulated motion; choose kinematic when you want scripted control but still need collision interaction.

Tuning Rigidbody properties transforms raw physics into usable gameplay. Mass controls how much force is required to change an object's velocity; heavier objects need more force to accelerate. Drag and angular drag simulate air resistance and rotational damping: add drag to slow sliding or to avoid perpetual motion after collisions. A practical pattern is to start with reasonable defaults, then adjust mass in proportion to expected forces. For example, if a player push applies a fixed impulse, increase the mass of heavy crates so they resist moving. The isKinematic flag is a special case: when set, the object no longer moves because of the physics simulation — you move it via script or animation — but it can still affect other non-kinematic rigidbodies through collisions. Use kinematic objects for moving platforms or doors that must be precisely controlled yet still interact with the player. A common misconception is treating drag as friction with the ground — drag is global velocity damping and not a substitute for friction between surfaces. When tuning, test collisions at runtime and observe relative velocity magnitudes to decide whether to apply impulses or alter mass and drag. Final takeaway: adjust these properties iteratively while playing the scene to find natural-feeling responses.

Colliders tell the physics engine where an object exists. Unity provides fast primitive colliders — BoxCollider, SphereCollider, and CapsuleCollider — and a MeshCollider for detailed shapes. Primitive colliders are computationally cheap and are the preferred choice for moving objects because they allow the physics solver to calculate collisions quickly. Use a BoxCollider for crates or floors, a SphereCollider for round pickups, and a CapsuleCollider for characters since its shape approximates a standing humanoid well and provides smooth sliding against obstacles. MeshColliders use the object's mesh geometry and can be either convex or non-convex; they give precise collisions but at a significant performance cost. Non-convex MeshColliders cannot be used on moving Rigidbodies that collide with other non-convex MeshColliders, so they are typically reserved for static environment geometry like terrain and large architecture. Best practice: approximate complex meshes with a compound of primitive colliders whenever possible. For example, approximate a car with several boxes and spheres rather than a single MeshCollider to keep collision checks fast. A misconception is that mesh colliders automatically give better gameplay; often they introduce jitter or performance spikes if used on dynamic objects. Takeaway: prefer primitives for moving objects, reserve mesh colliders for static, detailed geometry.

Unity provides two overlapping detection models: collision callbacks and trigger callbacks. Collision callbacks — OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit — are used when physical contact and response are important. They return a Collision object with contact points and relative velocity, which you can use to respond physically, play impact sounds, or apply forces. For instance, to make a ball bounce off a wall and play a sound when impact is strong, check the Collision's relativeVelocity magnitude inside OnCollisionEnter and add an impulse or play audio accordingly. Trigger callbacks — OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit — are for overlap detection without physical obstruction. A Collider marked as Is Trigger will let objects pass through while still notifying scripts. Use triggers for pickups, zones that damage the player, or finish lines because they detect entry without changing motion. A frequent error is forgetting that at least one of the interacting objects must have a Rigidbody for callbacks to fire. Also, triggers do not produce contact points or relative velocity; they are purely for detection logic. Takeaway: use collisions when you need physical response and use triggers when you only need to detect presence or overlaps.

Let's walk through a simple trigger script for collectibles. The script checks when another collider enters the trigger, verifies that it belongs to the player via a tag, and then runs collection logic such as awarding points or destroying the item. This pattern keeps item logic self-contained and minimizes coupling between player and items. In practice, ensure the player GameObject has a Rigidbody and the collectible's collider has Is Trigger enabled. Also confirm tags are consistent. A common mistake is relying solely on object names or lacking a tag check, which can produce false positives; use CompareTag for reliable checks. When destroying the item, you might want to play an effect first, so call the effect before Destroy. This example is safe for runtime usage and scales when you add pooling or UX feedback. Try extending the script to notify a score manager or emit an event instead of directly destroying the GameObject if you need decoupled systems. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Physics Materials let you control how colliders interact at their contact points. Two main properties are friction, which resists sliding between surfaces, and bounciness, which controls how much velocity is returned after a collision. Each material also has combine modes for friction and bounce — Average, Minimum, Multiply, and Maximum — that determine how two materials' properties mix on contact. For example, if one object has high bounciness and the other is low, the Bounce Combine mode determines whether the result is averaged, dominated by the maximum, or multiplied, which affects the final behavior. A practical example: an icy surface uses low friction to let objects slide, while a rubber ball uses high bounciness and a Maximum combine to keep lots of rebound energy. Avoid relying on physics materials alone to create directional bounces; use collision callbacks to add impulses for more control. Also note that 2D and 3D physics use different material asset types. Takeaway: use Physics Materials to define consistent surface interactions and choose combine modes intentionally when objects with different materials collide. Raycasting is a non-physical detection method that sends an invisible line into the scene and returns the first collider it intersects. Use it for line-of-sight checks, object selection, interaction prompts, and ground detection. A Physics. Raycast call returns a boolean indicating a hit and can populate a RaycastHit struct with the hit object, impact point, and surface normal. Raycasts are efficient and precise because you control origin, direction, distance, and layer filtering. For example, for object selection from the camera, create a ray from the camera's center forward and use a LayerMask to include only interactable objects; this prevents accidental hits on UI or environment geometry. A common pitfall is not using LayerMasks, which leads to hitting unintended objects and extra processing. Also, raycasts do not replace collisions for physical simulation — they are detection tools. When using raycasts for ground checks, prefer short rays and consider using multiple rays or a small sphere cast to avoid false negatives on uneven terrain. Takeaway: raycasts give precise, low-cost detection when you need to ask questions about the scene without altering physics state.

When things don't behave as expected, a few quick checks usually identify the problem. First, ensure at least one of the colliding or overlapping objects has a Rigidbody — without it, collision and trigger callbacks won't run. Second, verify that triggers have Is Trigger checked and that you are using the correct callback type: triggers use OnTriggerEnter while physical impacts use OnCollisionEnter. Third, confirm that you assigned the correct Physics Material type for 3D physics; using a 2D material will have no effect. Fourth, watch out for MeshColliders on moving objects — they often cause performance issues or unexpected interactions; prefer compound primitive colliders for moving elements. Fifth, use LayerMasks with raycasts to prevent hitting unintended objects and to speed up checks. Helpful debugging tools include Debug. DrawRay to visualize rays and adding Debug. Log statements that show collision. relativeVelocity to tune bounce thresholds. Finally, when destroying objects in triggers, consider playing visual or audio feedback first or use object pooling to avoid allocation spikes. Takeaway: systematic checks for Rigidbody presence, collider settings, material type, and layer masks will resolve most common physics problems.

Let's recap the most important terms you will use repeatedly. A Rigidbody hands control to Unity's physics engine so gravity, forces, and collisions change an object's motion. A Collider defines the physical volume used for collision detection; primitive colliders are fast and ideal for dynamic objects, while MeshColliders are precise but heavier. Collision Events like OnCollisionEnter provide contact data and are used when physical response is required. Trigger Events like OnTriggerEnter detect overlaps without blocking motion and are perfect for pickups and zones. These distinctions guide how you design interactive mechanics and tune performance. Keep these definitions in mind as you build scenes and debug behavior. Which of these would you check first when a pickup doesn't register — collider setup or Rigidbody presence? That quick check often fixes the issue.

Finish with three more concepts that shape interactive behavior. Physics Materials control friction and bounciness and include combine modes that determine how two materials mix at contact. Raycasting is an efficient way to query the scene along a line for object selection, line-of-sight checks, or precise ground detection; combine raycasts with LayerMasks for accuracy and performance. Interaction patterns like using an IInteractable interface keep object-specific logic decoupled from the player code, letting different objects implement their own behaviors when hit by a raycast. These patterns and assets let you create polished, responsive mechanics while staying mindful of performance.
